children.text: Sugar planter Mariano Lacson built this mansion in memory of the wife he lost, and a fire in
left only its concrete skeleton. It is
20–30 minutes
by car from Bacolod and is at its most beautiful at sunset and after dark, when the lights come on.

The Ruins is the skeleton of a two-story mansion standing in the middle of sugarcane fields in Talisay City, Negros Occidental. Sugar planter Don Mariano Ledesma Lacson built it in memory of his wife, Maria Braga, who died before him, which is why it is nicknamed the "Taj Mahal of Negros." It lies about
7km
northeast of downtown
Bacolod
and about
13km
southwest of Bacolod-Silay Airport, so it is easy to add at the end of a day in the city or on the way to or from the airport.
Mariano was the youngest of eight children and a younger brother of General Aniceto Lacson, who led the Negros Revolution of

. He married Maria Braga, a woman of Portuguese descent from Macau whom he met in Hong Kong, and they had ten children. According to the official account, Maria, pregnant with their eleventh child, slipped in the bathroom and was badly hurt; the doctor was in Silay, two days away by horse-drawn carriage, and she and the baby died before he arrived. Maria is said to have died in
, and the mansion is understood to have been built afterward, around
, beside Mariano's family home. The years differ slightly from source to source.

The mansion stood at the center of a plantation that covered about 440 hectares. Engineer Luis Puentevella is said to have designed it, while Mariano's son Felipe stayed on site as A-grade concrete was poured without a break. It had about 900㎡ of floor area and ten rooms, with an Italianate exterior of round arches and paired columns and shell-shaped ornaments along the roofline. In

, Filipino guerrillas, worried that the Japanese army would use the house as a headquarters, set it on fire with Mariano's consent; it burned for three days, consuming the roof and the thick wooden floors. Only the reinforced concrete walls and columns remained, and that is what you see today.
After that the house lay abandoned in the cane fields for more than 60 years, until Mariano's great-grandson Raymund Javellana took it over in
, landscaped the garden, and opened it to the public in
January 2008
. In

it was named best destination in the heritage category at the Choose Philippines Awards, and an overseas publication listed it among the 12 most fascinating ruins in the world. It is still private property run by descendants of the Lacson family, and once you pay admission you can walk freely through the mansion and its garden. A visit takes only
1–2 hours
, so it suits families who want to avoid long transfers, travelers who love photography, and anyone curious about the history of the Negros sugar industry.

blocks.title: The front view from the fountain

children.text: The spot in front of the four-tiered fountain at the edge of the lawn is the classic place to fit the whole mansion into one frame. The fountain is believed to be an original that survived along with the house, and each tier lights up after sunset. Shoot right after opening or on a weekday, when there are fewer people, for a clean background.

blocks.title: Finding the two M's on the columns

children.text: Look closely at the outer columns and you will see a repeated motif of two letter M's facing each other. They are the initials of Mariano and Maria, a sign of who this house was built for. Ask a guide and they will point out where the letters are easiest to see.

blocks.title: The shell-trimmed roofline and the west corner

children.text: Shell-shaped ornaments line the edge of the roof like a crown. The style was used on the homes of ship captains in New England in the United States, and it recalls Maria's father, who was a ship captain. On the west side of the second floor there is said to have been a lookout where the family watched the sunset.

The wooden second floor burned away, so from the ground floor you look up at walls and beams open to a height of two stories. Today a roof installed for events covers the space and chandeliers hang from it, while old patterned tiles that survived the fire remain on the floor. Portraits of the Lacson couple, old photographs, and a wooden cart are also on display.

On-site guides tell the story of the Lacson family and the fire with plenty of humor. This is also where you will hear that egg whites were mixed into the concrete to make the walls as smooth as marble, a family tradition that is not confirmed by any record.

blocks.title: The simborio, a chimney topped by a tree

children.text: A short distance south of the mansion stands the concrete chimney of an old muscovado sugar mill. It is called the simborio, and a tree has taken root on its top, so from a distance it looks like one tall tree. It is a reminder that this land was a sugar plantation.

When the western sky turns red, light passes through the empty windows and arches and the walls glow gold. After sunset, lights come on at the base of the walls and the mansion looks completely different from the daytime. Enter about
1 hour
before sunset and one ticket covers the daylight, the sunset, and the night view.

blocks.title: A garden stroll and the café

children.text: Walk the lawn garden and flower beds around the mansion, then rest at the café inside the mansion or the restaurant across the lawn. There is a souvenir shop near the entrance, and an 18-hole mini golf course is also mentioned, but check on site whether it is operating. The place is also very popular for weddings and wedding photo shoots.

items.subtitle: Daylight, sunset, and night view in one visit

children.text: Leave downtown Bacolod by taxi or Grab (about
20–30 minutes
). Arrange your ride back at this point.
Buy your ticket at the ticket office, go in, and see the interior, the portraits, and the old photographs while listening to the guide.
Walk once around the outside of the mansion, looking at the M motif on the columns, the shell ornaments on the roofline, and the west corner.
Walk to the simborio chimney on the south side, then come back to the garden.
Settle in front of the fountain and watch the mansion take on the colors of sunset.
Photograph the lit-up night view and rest over a drink at the café.
Before closing, take the ride you booked back to the city for dinner.

items.title: Morning route
items.subtitle: The quiet hour right after opening

children.text: If you want photos without people or have other plans in the afternoon, arrive at opening time. There is no sunset, but it is cooler than midday.
Arrive at opening and first photograph the front view from the fountain.
Listen to the guide and look around the interior and the exterior ornaments.
Walk to the simborio and around the garden, then take a short break at the café.
Head up to Silay to walk its street of old mansions, or return to downtown Bacolod for a chicken inasal lunch.

From Bacolod, follow Lacson Street north toward Talisay, pass the flyover in front of the Ceres North Terminal and the Pepsi plant, then turn right toward the mountains. Drive about

Signs lead the way from the junction, and there is a parking lot beside the entrance. Hiring a vehicle for half a day to combine The Ruins with Silay is also convenient.

There is no lodging at The Ruins, so most visitors stay in Bacolod. The Lacson Street area, lined with restaurants and cafés, is on the side of the city toward The Ruins and gives the shortest ride; mid-range hotels there cost about
per night. If you have an early morning flight, another option is to stay at a small hotel in Silay, where the airport is (about
per night), and see The Ruins the evening before.

The café inside the mansion serves drinks and snacks, and the restaurant across the lawn serves Filipino and Western dishes. On some evenings there is live piano or acoustic guitar. Prices are higher than at restaurants in the city and the menu changes, so check on site. Fittingly for a place in the middle of cane fields, it is also known for freshly pressed sugarcane juice, though it may not be sold every day. For a proper meal, the usual plan is to go back to Bacolod for charcoal-grilled chicken inasal, or to try the pies and pastries of a long-established bakery in Silay.
Opening hours are
daily. The site sometimes closes without notice for private events such as weddings, so check the
official website
or call (034) 476-9448 before you set out.
The best time to enter is
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
before sunset. You see the gray walls by day, the golden sunset, and the lit-up night in a single visit.
The guided talks are understood to be free of charge. There may be no fixed schedule, so ask at the entrance when the next one starts.
Show a student ID for the student discount and an ID card for the senior or disability discount. Children under 8 enter free when accompanied by a guardian.
Souvenir photos taken with a phone are included in the admission. For shoots with a photo crew, such as wedding or portrait sessions, pay the photo shoot fee separately and book ahead.
The front view photographs best from in front of the fountain, and the night view from the foot of the front steps, looking up.
If you combine it with Silay's street of old mansions on the same day, put Silay in the morning and The Ruins at sunset. The two are
20–30 minutes
apart by car.
Cash is easiest for tricycles, the ticket office, and the souvenir shop. Carry plenty of
, and
bills.
There is little shade during the day and there are mosquitoes in the evening. Bring a hat, water, and insect repellent, and pack a folding umbrella in the rainy season.

The Ruins is a ruined structure that has stood in wind and rain for more than 80 years. Do not climb or lean on the walls, railings, or window frames, and stay out of closed-off areas and off the stairs leading to the upper level. If you are with children, hold their hands.
After dark, the approach road through the cane fields is unlit and few vehicles pass. Do not walk out to the main road; always arrange your ride back in advance.
On event days, parts of the garden or interior are blocked off and there are fewer places to take photos. Before making a long trip, confirm that the site is open to regular visitors that day.
Kanlaon Volcano (about
37km
to the southeast) has erupted repeatedly since
June 2024
and was at Alert Level 2 as of early
October 2026
. Flights are canceled when ash spreads, so check the latest notices from PHIVOLCS and your airline.
Tricycles have no fixed fare table, and drivers sometimes quote tourists a high price. Before you get in, make clear whether the fare is per vehicle or per person.
Do not write on the walls or touch the ornaments. If you want to fly a drone or do a commercial shoot, ask the management office in advance.
